What predicts choosing full-time social action?

A plain-language report for the NGO. The first half is written for anyone who knows the programme. The second half adds the technical detail.

1. The question the NGO asked

"What predicts the choosing of 'Full-time' engagement in social action by a participant in his / her last attended workshop?"

In NIRMAN terms: before and after a workshop, each participant is asked how they plan to engage in social action. "Full-time" means they picked "Fulltime as a career". We looked at what is known before the workshop and asked which of it tells us who picks full-time afterwards. We used Batches 11 to 17 and the first (Point 1) workshop.

2. The short answer

Where a participant starts is the best clue to where they end up.

Nine in ten of those who already wanted a full-time social career still did afterwards. Among those who did not, about four in ten moved to full-time.

What people rank highly before the workshop, such as working in an NGO or social entrepreneurship, adds a smaller hint. Spotting in advance who will change their mind is much harder.

This describes patterns, not causes. We have no comparison group, so we cannot say the workshop itself caused any change.

For NIRMAN programme directors: what this means

NIRMAN, run by SEARCH with MKCL, aims to build a lasting community of young people who work full or part time for social change. This analysis asks a narrow, practical question inside that mission: when a participant leaves a workshop wanting to make social action a full-time career, what was already true about them at the start?

Where the question sits in a participant's journey

So "last attended workshop" effectively means Point 1, because the later workshops in Batches 11 to 17 cannot be compared before and after. The answer "Fulltime as a career" is a stated plan at the gate, not yet a career.

How the answer was built: widen, then stress-test

Step 1: a small first look, one workshop batch (Batch 14)148 people
Result: a real, lopsided shift towards full-time. 40 people moved in, 2 moved out.

Result: all five agree the finding is broadly supported. They used the same data, so this shows consistency, not proof.

What it could mean for the programme (ideas to discuss)

The workshop keeps its committed core

One in four participants (365 of 1,450) arrives wanting full-time, and 92% of them still do after the workshop.

It also moves many who are still deciding

About 4 in 10 of those who did not start full-time (431 of 1,085) chose full-time afterwards. Several things could explain this besides the workshop, so we do not claim the workshop caused it.

The Pre survey is an early signal, not a gate

A strong ranking of NGO work and social entrepreneurship at the start is the clearest early hint. The reports advise against treating a low ranking as a "no".

The next question for NIRMAN

This study stops at the end of Point 1. The participant records also hold current work status and years of social action. Linking plans to those later outcomes is a natural follow-up, though it would need care because those fields are incomplete.

How five different reasoning paths reached the same answer

From Step 3, the answer consistency report

Step 3 did not simply repeat the analysis. It asked five independent "teams" to test the Step 2 conclusion, each using a different way of reasoning. If the answer were a fluke of one method, the teams would disagree. All five reached the same verdict: "broadly supported".

Picture five assessors visiting the same programme. One counts heads, one asks "would this still hold if we had surveyed different people?", one checks village by village, one ignores the loudest and quietest voices, and one plays twenty questions. If they all point to the same finding, you can trust it more.

Run 1: the standard way

The accountant's ledger

Plain percentages, how far apart groups are, and a model on standardized scores. This gave the reference answer.

Validated: 92% of Pre full-timers stay, 40% of the others move, and starting status ranks first. Accuracy 0.77 overall, 0.64 for movers.
Run 2: no assumptions

Re-running the survey many times

The career questions are rankings, so this run used medians and rank tests, and re-sampled the data to see whether the numbers wobble.

Validated: the answer is stable. Stay rate 0.92 (range 0.90 to 0.95) and move rate 0.40 (range 0.37 to 0.43). Every direction held, overall and among movers.
Run 3: batch by batch

Checking every village before trusting the district average

Batches differ in size and in their usual full-time rate. This run weighed each batch fairly so one big batch could not drive the result.

Validated: the pattern holds inside each batch, not just overall. Odds ratio for starting status 19.6 before and about 9.6 after adjusting for batch. Movers 0.65.
Run 4: ignore the extremes

Marking an exam on questions the student never saw

It trimmed unusual answers and scored a cautious model only on people held back from learning, so stayers could not flatter the result.

Validated: the finding survives removing extremes. Starting status still ranks first on two separate importance measures. Movers 0.63.
Run 5: twenty questions

Which question does a simple decision tree ask first?

A small decision tree and a tiny learning model, then a check of whether five different ways of ranking the predictors give the same order.

Validated: starting status comes first under all four ranking measures. 93% stay and 38% move, on a smaller group of 1,290. Movers 0.64.

Five roads, one destination

Each road is one reasoning path. The sign on each road shows the check it passed on the way. They start from different tools and still arrive at the same verdict. They share the same data, so this shows consistency, not independent proof.

What was validated, and what was not

Validated
  • Starting status is the strongest predictor of choosing full-time afterwards.
  • About 92% of those already full-time stay, and about 40% of the rest move.
  • Leaning towards NGO work and social entrepreneurship goes with choosing full-time. Leaning towards private or government jobs goes the other way.
  • Among movers the effects shrink to about half but keep their direction.
  • Overall accuracy is about 0.77, and about 0.63 to 0.65 among movers.
Qualified or not shown
  • "Mostly predicted by where you started" is slightly too strong. Remove starting status and accuracy drops only about 0.02.
  • The claim that all four preferences rank straight after starting status holds only in part. NGO and government matter most. The other two overlap and add little.
  • All five runs use the same data, so agreement shows consistency, not independent proof.
  • Association only. It does not show that the workshop caused the change.

3. The end-to-end process

Think of it like checking a new recipe. First we try it in one kitchen (one batch). Then we cook it in every kitchen (all batches). Then we cook it in a kitchen the recipe was never tuned for, to see whether it still works. Finally, five separate teams taste it and compare notes.

4. The simplified answer

People who arrive ready, stay ready

337 of 365 people (92%) who already wanted full-time still did after the workshop.

Like a seed that has already sprouted: it keeps growing.

A good share of the others come round to full-time

431 of 1,085 people (about 40%) who did not want full-time did afterwards. In Batch 14 alone, full-time went from about 1 in 5 people to nearly 1 in 2.

Many people who were still deciding moved towards full-time.

Early leanings are a compass, not a map

People who ranked "working in an NGO" or "social entrepreneurship" higher beforehand were more likely to choose full-time. People who ranked private-industry or government jobs higher were less likely. These hints are smaller than the starting point.

Who will change their mind is hard to call in advance

Among people who did not start out wanting full-time, our best prediction scores about 0.64 on a scale where 0.5 is a coin toss and 1.0 is perfect.

Like forecasting the weather weeks ahead: better than guessing, but not something to bet one person's future on.

Some batches look different from others

The share choosing full-time afterwards was lowest in Batch 14 (44.6%) and Batch 15 (46.4%), and highest in Batch 16 (61.3%) and Batch 17 (59.8%). The reports say this could come from a different mix of participants, different survey versions or different facilitators, so it should not be read as "later batches are better".

What does not seem to matter much

Life satisfaction, work satisfaction and financial security showed almost no difference between future full-timers and the rest. Expected income at age 30 had no clear link either: the middle expected income was about Rs 80,000 for full-timers against Rs 1,00,000 overall.

Mindset questions, such as picturing oneself in a social-sector career, looked promising. But they were asked in only a few batches, so the result is "not enough evidence", not "no effect".

What we cannot say

The data shows who ends up choosing full-time. It does not prove why. A person's answer is a stated plan right after the workshop, not a confirmed career. The analysis rates its own confidence at 58%.

What this suggests for the programme

This is our plain-language reading of the practical takeaways in the Step 2 report.

  • Use early NGO leaning as a useful early signal of who is heading towards full-time social action.
  • Do not write off someone with a low preference. About 4 in 10 of those who were not full-time at the start moved towards it.
  • Compare batches with care, and ask the same mindset questions in every batch so they can be tested properly.
  • Re-run the model checks before relying on the model. Part of the Step 2 analysis could not be confirmed.

8. How we arrived at the answer

We did not answer in one go. Each stage produced an output, and that output became the input of the next stage. This is how the answer was built.

Human question

What predicts choosing full-time social action at a participant's last workshop?

▼The question is split into a small first test

Step 1: Multi-Step Discovery module

Localized Batch 14 exploration. Did career plans change at all? (Step 1 report)

▼

Answer

Yes. Full-time rose from 18.92% to 44.59% in Batch 14: 40 people moved in and 2 moved out. The effect is real and lopsided.

▼The matching rules proved in Step 1 (pair each person's before and after, count "Fulltime as a career") are reused. The new question is: does it hold in every batch?

Step 2: Multi-Step Discovery module

Global cohort data audit and variable shortlisting for Batches 11 to 17. (Step 2 report)

▼

Broad answer

Where people start comes first, and an NGO or social-entrepreneurship leaning comes second. Only 5 core features were clean enough to use, on 1,450 people (1,183 in the model).

▼The broad answer, as written, becomes the input for Step 3: "validate the broad conclusion".

Validation (Step 3)

Five independent checks re-ran the conclusion and tested it on batches not used for learning. (Step 3 report)

▼

Validated answer

Broadly supported. Starting status ranks first and NGO-leaning preferences second. Predicting who will change their mind has a ceiling of about 0.64 AUC.

What the tree shows
  • Each choice shaped the next stage. Choosing to validate first led to a verified cohort. Choosing a lean, redundancy-checked model led to the model rebuild. Choosing to stress-test on switchers led to Step 5.
  • The path was careful rather than fast. Every choice taken was a "check it properly" option. Three of the five were re-runs.
  • Only two of five stages returned numbers (Steps 2 and 4). The other three showed no output, which is a main reason the Step 2 report rates its own confidence at 58%.
  • Three trails were never taken at each fork, such as studying only the movers early, or stopping to write up with caveats. They remain open for a next round.

Questions people asked, in plain words

The reports keep a log of follow-up questions. These are the most useful ones, answered simply. The two most useful full answers are previewed below.

Why does "where you started" come out on top?

The same question was asked before and after, and people tend to stay with a commitment once they have made it. The gap between the two groups is about 53 points: 92% against 40%.

Like a race: most people finish near where they began.

Does it just reflect the people who stayed?

Partly. The 337 people who stayed make up 44% of everyone who chose full-time afterwards. The other 56% were movers. That is why the stayers make any prediction look more accurate than it is, and why the movers-only figure is the fairer test.

Do career preferences still matter once we know the starting point?

Yes, but less. Working in an NGO is the most consistent second place, and a government job preference is usually third. Social entrepreneurship and private-industry preferences overlap with the NGO one, so they add little on their own. Among movers only, the effects are about half as large.

How well can we predict who will change their mind?

Modestly. Among people who started out not full-time, the Step 3 analysis scores about 0.63 to 0.65. The Step 2 model scored lower, about 0.6. Both are above a coin toss (0.5) and well below perfect (1.0).

Is "mostly predicted by where you started" too strong?

Slightly. Taking away the starting status only drops accuracy from about 0.77 to about 0.75, because career preferences partly reflect where people already stood. Step 3 therefore calls the claim "broadly supported, with qualifications".

Why only 58% confident in Step 2?

Part of the analysis (the later model steps) did not return results, so the odds ratios could not be independently confirmed. Group sizes also differ between checks (1,450, 1,290, 1,183 and about 860), and the way "Not yet decided / confused" is counted changes them.

The five checks, explained simply

Check 1

The standard way

Plain percentages, gaps between groups, and a model on standardized scores. It gave the reference answer: 92% stay, 40% move, 44% of full-timers were stayers. It rated the claim as met on 6 of 7 criteria.

Check 2

Without assumptions

Because the career questions are rankings, this check used medians and rank-based tests and re-sampled the data to see whether the "about 4 in 10" figure is stable. It is: 37% to 43%.

Check 3

Fair across batches

This check compared like with like, batch by batch, so one large batch could not dominate. The starting-status effect stayed very large (an odds ratio of about 19.6 before batch adjustment).

Check 4

Ignore the extremes

It trimmed unusual values and used a model that holds back from over-fitting, then checked which answers mattered most. Trimming makes gaps look bigger, so those numbers are not stronger evidence.

Check 5

A simple decision tree

A small decision tree and a tiny learning model on a smaller group (1,290 people, dropping those who were unsure). It found the same pattern: 93% stay and 38% move.

All five agree, but they all use the same data. Agreement shows the result is consistent, not that it is proven.

About the data

  • Programme: NIRMAN is SEARCH's youth social-leadership programme. It identifies and supports young people towards social-change careers.
  • Survey table: 4,304 before-and-after survey responses from 2,177 participants, with 181 questions on career preferences, life priorities, worries, money and about 14 mindset themes. It covers Batches 7 to 17.
  • Participant table: 2,890 participants across Batches 1 to 17, with facts such as gender, education and current work.
  • The key question: "How do you plan to engage in social action?" Options run from "Monetary contribution" up to "Fulltime as a career". "Not yet decided / confused" is treated as not answered in some analyses and as not full-time in others.
  • Career preference questions are rankings from 1 to 8 where a lower number means a stronger preference. We flipped them so that higher means stronger.
  • Single group, no comparison: everyone attended. So we report associations and change, never proof that the workshop caused it.

The conclusion in detail

  • Starting point matters most. Of 365 people already choosing full-time before the workshop, 337 (92%) chose it again afterwards. Of 1,085 who were not, 431 (about 40%) moved to full-time.
  • Career leanings are a real but smaller signal. People who ended up full-time had ranked working in an NGO (+0.71) and social entrepreneurship (+0.61) higher beforehand, and private-industry (-0.42) and government jobs (-0.38) lower. These are effect sizes (Cohen's d).
  • Changing minds is hard to predict. Looking only at people who started out not full-time, the model reaches about 0.63 to 0.65 AUC.
  • Batches differ. The full-time rate at Post runs from 44.6% (Batch 14) to 61.3% (Batch 16).
  • Overall verdict: "broadly supported", with 58% confidence stated in the Step 2 report.

How we answered it: three rounds

Round 1

Did anything change? (Step 1 report)

We looked at one group, Batch 14. Full-time intent rose from 18.92% before the workshop to 44.59% after, among 148 people. The shift was lopsided: 40 people switched into full-time and only 2 switched out.

Round 2

Does it hold across time? (Step 2 report)

We scaled up to Batches 11 to 17, with 1,450 matched before-and-after pairs. 768 of them (52.97%) chose full-time afterwards. The full data was messy because survey questions changed over the years, so we kept a smaller set of well-filled columns and sub-cohorts. The model sample was 1,183 people.

Round 3

Validation (Step 3 report)

We ran the exact model and tested it on batches it had not seen. The conclusion was broadly supported. Overall accuracy was about 0.77 AUC, about 0.75 without the starting status, and about 0.63 to 0.65 for people who started out not full-time.

The step-by-step method

  1. Pin down the question and the definitions."Full-time" means the answer "Fulltime as a career" at the end of the workshop. Every other answer counts as not full-time. Each person's before (Pre) and after (Post) answers are paired. The last workshop is taken as the highest level attended, and only the Point 1 workshop (Level 0.1) is used.
  2. Round 1: test one batch (Step 1 report).Batch 14 has 148 matched people. Full-time intent rose from 28 people to 66. Five separate checks, including a McNemar test (p < 0.01), a duplicate audit and a bootstrap, all gave the same numbers. Caveat: they all use the same data and rules, so this confirms the arithmetic, not the data itself.
  3. Round 2a: scale up and audit the data (Step 2 report).Across Batches 11 to 17 there are 1,491 people, of whom 1,450 have a usable Pre and Post pair. Many survey questions changed between years, so no one answered all 16 candidate fields.
  4. Round 2b: screen for signals.Compare people who ended up full-time with those who did not, using the answers they gave before the workshop. NGO work and social entrepreneurship stand out most. Answers given after the workshop are excluded, because they would leak the outcome.
  5. Round 2c: shortlist clean columns.Keep a near-complete block of five features: the four career preferences (ranks flipped so higher means stronger) plus the log of expected income at age 30. This keeps 1,183 people. A stricter group of about 860 is used to study movers.
  6. Round 2d: build the model.A regularized logistic regression, tested by leaving one whole batch out at a time. This asks whether the model works on a batch it has never seen. AUC was 0.776 against 0.675 for a baseline using starting status and batch only.
  7. Round 3: validate (Step 3 report).Five independent analyses re-ran the conclusion: a parametric baseline, a non-parametric one, a batch-stratified one, a trimmed and regularized one, and a decision tree. All agreed that starting status is first and NGO-leaning preferences are second. Stripping out the stayers, the movers-only AUC falls to about 0.63 to 0.65.
  8. Check the limits.There is no comparison group, "full-time" is a stated plan and not a verified career, and group sizes differ between runs. So the result is reported as an association with stated confidence.

Plain-words glossary

Pre and Post
The survey taken before the workshop and the one taken right after it.
Matched pair
One person's Pre and Post answers, linked together by their participant ID.
Switcher or mover
Someone who was not full-time before and chose full-time after.
AUC
How well a prediction ranks people correctly. 0.5 is a coin toss and 1.0 is perfect.
Cohen's d ("gap")
How far apart two groups are on one answer. About 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large.
Odds ratio
How many times more (or less) likely something is. 10 means ten times as likely.
Leave-one-batch-out
Test the model on a batch it never saw while learning. It is like trying a recipe in a new kitchen.

What the reports recommend next

  • Reconcile the group sizes (1,450, 1,290, 1,183 and about 860) and always state which one a number uses.
  • Re-run the model on the 1,085 people who started out not full-time, validating by leaving out one batch at a time.
  • Check each batch separately, and flag groups smaller than 100 people.
  • Treat the mindset questions as a low-coverage side check, since they were asked in only some batches.
  • Look at secondary outcomes: life-satisfaction gains of 2 or more points, and whether "cause of work" moved up each person's ranking.

Things to keep in mind

  • Different figures use different group sizes (148, 1,450, 1,183 and about 860), so always check which group a number refers to.
  • The Step 2 report rates its own confidence at 58% and calls its model odds ratios unverified.
  • The Step 3 report is titled "Validated Answer", but its verdict is "broadly supported", not proven.
  • The Step 1 report treats the answer "Not yet decided / confused" two ways, as missing in one section and as a valid non-full-time answer in the runs. This changes group sizes and should be settled.
  • Starting status inflates accuracy. Without it, AUC drops only about 0.02, because career preferences partly reflect where people already stood. The movers-only figure is the fairer test.
  • Income data is weak: only about 1,320 usable values, many rounded.
